pll1d14c2-d1e3477.summary: Reports the view that the Spirit himself, God, is not given, but only his gifts, which are not he, and that the Spirit is said to be given when his grace is given; this view is attributed to Bede's words.

pll1d14c2-d1e3483.summary: Refutes the view with De Trinitate XV: the same Spirit given when Jesus breathed and at Pentecost is the Spirit into whose name we baptize. How great is the God who gives God? So the Spirit himself, God, is given by Father and Son.
claims: The Spirit given by Christ's breath and at Pentecost is the Spirit himself.

pll1d14c2-d1e3513.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Spiritu sancto I: though many are called spirits, God's Spirit is one, received by apostles and prophets, the one Spirit we have drunk (1 Cor 12:13), who cannot be divided but is poured into souls. He is neither of corporeal nor of invisible creaturely substance. So the uncreated Spirit himself is infused into minds.
claims: The Spirit of God is one and indivisible.
The Spirit is poured into souls.
The Spirit is not a creature.

pll1d14c2-d1e3553.summary: Further Ambrose: every creature is mutable, but not the Spirit. He is given (Rom 5:5), inaccessible by nature yet receivable by goodness, filling all by power, participated only by the just, simple yet rich in virtues, present to each and everywhere whole. Angels were sent to few, the Spirit poured into peoples at once, which only the divine can do. So the one simple Spirit is given to many.
claims: The Spirit is immutable, unlike every creature.
The Spirit is inaccessible by nature yet receivable by his goodness.
The Spirit is wholly present everywhere and to each.
Being poured into many at once is proper to the divine.

pll1d14c2-d1e3613.summary: Cites Augustine's sermon on Rom 5:5: God gives the Holy Spirit, a gift such as he himself is. Great is his mercy: he gives a gift equal to himself.
claims: God gives a gift equal to himself, the Holy Spirit.

pll1d14c2-d1e3649.summary: Concludes that the Spirit, equal to Father and Son, is given to us, and yet is not lesser, since, as Augustine says, being sent by Father and Son does not make him lesser.
claims: The Spirit, equal to Father and Son, is given to us.
Being sent does not make the Spirit lesser.

pl-l1d14c2.summary: Rejects the view that only the Spirit's gifts, not the Spirit himself, are given, which some read into Bede. With Augustine, the very Spirit given when Jesus breathed and at Pentecost is God, and only God can give God. With Ambrose, the one Spirit, not a creature and unchangeable, is poured into minds, wholly present to each, given to many at once, which shows his divinity. With Augustine on Rom 5:5, God gives a gift equal to himself, the Spirit. That the Spirit is sent and given by Father and Son does not make him lesser.
claims: The Holy Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given to humans.
The one who gives God must be God.
The Spirit is poured into minds while remaining one, undivided, and unchangeable.
Being given to many at once shows the Spirit's divinity.
The gift God gives is equal to himself, the Holy Spirit.
Being sent or given does not make the Spirit lesser than Father and Son.
